name: Aaron Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Aaron. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run CNC lathes at a firm that makes pump parts, mostly brass and steel valve bodies for water systems. CNC means the machine's run by a computer program, so my job's loading the bar stock, setting the tools, checking the first parts with a micrometer, and keeping it fed. On a good day I've got three machines humming and I'm walking between them with a coffee. On a bad day a tool snaps at seven in the morning and the whole batch is scrap.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who do you work with, and what's life like outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: There's about forty of us on the floor, and the setter, Kev, is the one who taught me most of what I know. I'm a shop steward for our union, which mostly means I'm the one people moan to about the rota. Outside work I live with my girlfriend Leila, she teaches at a nursery, and we're saving for a deposit on a flat. We've got about three months of bills put by, plus what's in the deposit pot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now can we talk about pay again. Half the reason management never gave us a decent rise is they kept saying the robots were coming. I'd say that at the next union meeting, word for word.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, it means I keep my job and get a bit more confident about buying a flat. I already use one of those chat AI things now and then to help write grievance letters, so I'd keep doing that. Nothing big changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep on as I am, and Leila and I would probably put an offer in on a flat within the year. I'd push the union to go for a proper pay claim, five or six percent. Maybe I'd do the setter course Kev keeps nagging me about, just for the extra money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit cheated, maybe, after all the scary talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the robots were used as a reason not to raise pay. Can you give me an example?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last year's pay talks, the manager actually put up a slide with a robot arm on it. He said every penny had to go to “future proofing”. Then nothing was bought, and our rise was two percent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would buying the flat mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad rented his whole life and was always scared of the landlord. Having my own front door would mean I'm not that. It's the main thing Leila and I talk about at night.

S0.say: I'd say good, now let's talk about pay, because management kept using the threat of robots to hold down our rises. I'd say it word for word at the next union meeting.
S0.think: It means I keep my job and feel safer about buying a flat. I'd keep using AI now and then for grievance letters, but nothing big would change.
S0.do: Carries on at the lathes and puts an offer in on a flat with Leila within the year. Pushes the union for a pay claim of five or six percent and may take the setter course.
S0.feel: Calm, with a touch of feeling cheated after all the scary talk.
S0.quote: Last year's pay talks, the manager actually put up a slide with a robot arm on it.
S0.fieldNote: Aaron reads the robot talk as a bargaining tactic used against workers. His real goal is buying a flat, which ties back to his father renting all his life. As a shop steward he thinks in pay claims and grievance letters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the union has to negotiate the change, not just fight it. If they're bringing in robots to load the lathes, we want training, we want the new jobs offered to us first, and we want a share of the savings. I'd post that in our members' group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, loading bar stock is the bit a robot does easily, I've seen it at trade shows. Setting and fixing the machines is harder. So I think the people who can set and program survive, and the people who just load and watch don't, and right now I'm about halfway between.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finally do the setter course, and then the robot programming course at the college once a couple of the lads had done it and said it was worth it. That's about eight hundred I'd ask the firm to pay for. I'd hold off on the flat for six months to see where it lands, and keep pushing the union for a training deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not scared. It's a change I can see coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait till a couple of others had done the course. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've been burned. I paid for a forklift ticket at twenty-two thinking it'd open doors, and I've used it twice. Now I wait till I see someone actually get a better job from it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would holding off on the flat cause any tension at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Leila's ready now and her job's safer than mine, nobody wants a robot running a nursery. She'd say we're being too careful, and she'd probably be right, but I'd want six months.

S1.say: I'd say the union has to negotiate the change, not just fight it: training, first pick of new jobs and a share of the savings. I'd post that in our members' group chat.
S1.think: Loading bar stock is easy for a robot, but setting and fixing machines is harder. I'm about halfway between the people who'd survive and the people who wouldn't.
S1.do: Takes the setter course and then a robot programming course at the college once colleagues vouch for it, asking the firm to pay about 800. Delays the flat purchase six months and pushes for a union training deal.
S1.feel: Uneasy but not scared, because he can see the change coming.
S1.quote: I paid for a forklift ticket at twenty-two thinking it'd open doors, and I've used it twice.
S1.fieldNote: Aaron wants to move but only after proof, which he explains with a concrete story about a wasted forklift ticket. He sees a clear line between setters and loaders and places himself honestly in the middle. The flat delay shows his caution creating small strain at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need emergency rules: no mass layoffs without notice, and a tax on the companies selling the robots to pay for people's wages while things settle. I'd be on every union call. I'd probably end up shouting at someone on the local news page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it can do anything a person can do, then the setter course doesn't save me either. I'd be gone in a year or so, maybe less. Leila might last longer, but I wouldn't bet much on anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stop the flat, full stop, and keep the deposit as our emergency fund, that turns three months of cushion into more like a year. I'd go to every union meeting and help organise for a proper notice period and pay-outs. I'd vote and campaign for whoever backs a basic income, even though I used to think that was a fantasy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like a bad shift that doesn't end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years isn't much warning. What would you do in the first month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sit down with Leila and the bank app and work out exactly how long we'd last. Then I'd call Kev, because he's fifty-two and he'd be in a worse spot than me. And I'd stop buying anything that isn't food or bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a basic income used to sound like a fantasy. What changed in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If there's no work for anyone, then telling people to go and get a job is just cruel. In the slower picture I'd want training. Here there's nothing to train for, so the money has to come from somewhere.

S2.say: I'd call for emergency rules: no mass layoffs without notice, and a tax on robot sellers to cover people's wages. I'd be on every union call and probably arguing on the local news page.
S2.think: If AI can do anything a person can, even the setter course won't save me, and I'd be gone within about a year. Leila might last longer, but I wouldn't bet on it.
S2.do: Drops the flat purchase and turns the deposit into an emergency fund, stretching his cushion to about a year. Organises with the union for notice periods and pay-outs and campaigns for a basic income.
S2.feel: Alarmed, like a bad shift that never ends.
S2.quote: If there's no work for anyone, then telling people to go and get a job is just cruel.
S2.fieldNote: The deposit pot changes Aaron's position a lot here: he can stretch his cushion to about a year. He's thinking of Kev before himself in the first month. His view on basic income shifts openly, and he explains why rather than just flipping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan if the government starts now. Training, notice, a fund, all the stuff I'd demand in the fast one, but done calmly. I'd say it in meetings, not shouting online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like I said with the steady one, the setters last longer than the loaders. So maybe I'd get three or four years in a better role before the end point. It's not safe, but it's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the setter course straight away this time, no waiting for others, and then the robot programming one. I'd keep the deposit untouched for two years and decide then. I'd also ask the union to set up a hardship fund with the company now, while there's still money coming in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. But it's the kind of anxious where you've got a list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do the course straight away this time. That's different from before. What's changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the steady one I could afford to wait and see who did well. Here the clock's ticking, and if I wait a year I've wasted a fifth of it. I'd still grumble about it, mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Leila about the flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her not yet, and that I'm not saying never. If by year two it looks like people are still getting work, we'd buy. If not, we'd be glad we kept the money.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to plan if the government starts now: training, notice and a fund, done calmly. I'd make the case in meetings rather than shouting online.
S3.think: Setters last longer than loaders, so I might get three or four years in a better role before the end point. It isn't safe, but it's time.
S3.do: Takes the setter course right away, then robot programming, without waiting for others. Keeps the deposit untouched for two years and asks the union to set up a hardship fund with the company.
S3.feel: Anxious, but the kind of anxious that comes with a to-do list.
S3.quote: Here the clock's ticking, and if I wait a year I've wasted a fifth of it.
S3.fieldNote: Aaron's usual wait-for-proof habit breaks once the timeline is fixed, and he explains the maths himself. He links the decision on the flat to what he sees by year two. His union instinct turns to building a hardship fund while money still comes in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so let's use it: retraining paid by the companies, shorter weeks so the work gets shared, and pensions sorted. I'd say that's the union's job now. I'd probably try to get it on the agenda at the regional conference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's actually not bad. I'd be thirty-seven, I'd have time to get good at programming robots and fixing them. Even if they end up fixing themselves, I'd have had a career out of it first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the flat with Leila this year, because a mortgage paid down for ten years is something. I'd do the setter course, then robot programming within two years, and try to move to maintenance. I'd push for a shorter working week in our next agreement so the work gets shared out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine. It's long enough that I can actually plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't buying a flat a risk if your job ends in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but renting's a risk too. If I'm paying off a mortgage for ten years while I've still got work, I own more of it by the end. My dad would have killed for ten years' notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should pay for the retraining?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The companies that buy the robots, and the ones that make them. They're the ones saving money. Not me out of my deposit, and not the taxpayer on their own.

S4.say: I'd say we've got a decade, so let's use it: company-paid retraining, shorter weeks to share the work, and pensions sorted. I'd try to get it on the agenda at the regional union conference.
S4.think: For me it's not bad, because at thirty-seven I'd have had time to get good at programming and fixing robots. Even if they end up fixing themselves, I'd have had a career first.
S4.do: Buys the flat with Leila this year and takes the setter course, then robot programming within two years, aiming for a maintenance role. Pushes for a shorter working week in the next union agreement.
S4.feel: Uneasy but mostly fine, because the timeline lets him plan.
S4.quote: My dad would have killed for ten years' notice.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years flips Aaron's flat decision: he'd buy now and pay it down while he has work. His plan blends personal retraining with a collective push for a shorter week. He is firm that companies, not workers, should fund retraining.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, by 2028. Kev would have nowhere to go, and I'd be throwing my deposit at the rent. What would help is notice, real notice, plus a fund paid by the companies so people get wages while they work out the next thing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what we'd want the new jobs to look like. Everyone talks about losing jobs, nobody asks us what we'd want instead. I'd want to keep making things, even if I'm the one telling the robot what to make.

headlineQuote: I'd want to keep making things, even if I'm the one telling the robot what to make.
portrait: Aaron Walsh, 27, runs CNC lathes making pump valve bodies and is a union shop steward. He lives with his girlfriend Leila, a nursery teacher, and the two are saving for a flat, a goal shaped by his father renting all his life. He's careful with change and normally waits until colleagues prove a course is worth it, after a wasted forklift ticket taught him that lesson. Calm if AI fizzles and alarmed by AGI in two years, he becomes more decisive as the timeline gets clearer, retraining straight away with five years and buying the flat with ten.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because his mentor Kev would have nowhere to go and his own deposit would vanish into rent.
whatWouldHelp: Real notice before layoffs, plus a fund paid by companies so people keep getting wages while they work out what comes next.
